crossLanguage.detail: None of these languages Title Case headings or buttons. Capitalising Every Word is one of the fastest tells of an unlocalised page. Sentence case only. (Thai, Chinese, Arabic, Persian and Urdu have no case at all, so the English design's capitalisation-based hierarchy has to be rebuilt from weight and size in five of nine locales.)

crossLanguage.issue: Latin punctuation left in non-Latin scripts
crossLanguage.detail: Armenian sentences end with ։ not '.'; Urdu with ۔ not '.'. Arabic, Persian and Urdu use ، ؛ ؟ not , ; ?. Chinese uses full-width 。， 、 ； ：（）. Each of these is a single-character change that disproportionately affects perceived quality.

crossLanguage.issue: letter-spacing / tracking inherited from the Latin design
crossLanguage.detail: CSS letter-spacing breaks the cursive joins of Arabic-script text, shattering words into disconnected letters. Any global tracking rule must be scoped away from ar/fa/ur. This is the single most visually destructive CSS property on this site.

crossLanguage.issue: Bidi mishandling of embedded Latin runs
crossLanguage.detail: Every RTL sentence on this site will contain Latin/numeric runs: NDA, PET, CNC, T1, PCO 1881, 0.15 mm, 500 t, 1.2344, DIN 16742. Without bidi isolation the algorithm strands parentheses, slashes, hyphens and units on the wrong side. Wrap them (<bdi> or dir="ltr" spans) and visually verify each pattern. Test strings: 'قالب 8 حفره‌ای', 'قوة الإطباق 500 t', 'PET پری فارم', 'اتفاقية عدم الإفصاح (NDA)'.

crossLanguage.issue: Number separators wrong for the locale
crossLanguage.detail: Turkish and Iranian Persian: period = thousands, comma = decimal (1.000 and 0,15). Russian and Armenian: thin space = thousands, comma = decimal (1 000 and 0,15). English/Thai/Chinese/Arabic/Urdu: comma = thousands, point = decimal. Rendering '1,000+ projects' unchanged into Turkish states 'more than one project'.

crossLanguage.issue: Font falls back to a default system face
crossLanguage.detail: Six of nine locales need a genuinely different font family. Armenian and Thai fall back to system faces that clash with the Latin design; Chinese may resolve to a JAPANESE face (wrong glyph forms for 直, 骨, 今); Persian may resolve to an Arabic face lacking پ چ ژ گ and using Arabic ک/ی forms; Urdu may resolve to Arabic Naskh, which reads as 'this is Arabic, not for us'.

crossLanguage.issue: Explaining the basics to expert markets
crossLanguage.detail: Türkiye (Bursa, Konya, İstanbul), China, Iran (Tehran, Tabriz) and Russia all have substantial domestic mould-making sectors. Introductory copy explaining what injection moulding is will read as condescending. Speak peer to peer: steel grades, cavitation, cycle time, tonnage, tool life in shots.

crossLanguage.issue: Reverse engineering framed without an IP guard
crossLanguage.detail: In these markets the phrase can carry an implication of copying someone else's product. Always pair it on-screen with the confidentiality/NDA message and frame it explicitly as recreating the customer's own part from their own sample.

CAD, CAM, CNC, DFM, NDA, RFQ, PET, EDM, T1 and steel grades (P20, H13, 1.2344, S136) and neck standards (PCO 1881) must stay Latin in all nine. Armenian Wikipedia titles its CAD article simply 'CAD'; Urdu's کمپیوٹر امدادی ڈیزائن is a coinage no engineer uses. Localising these makes the page both unidiomatic and unsearchable.

perLanguageTop.en: Choosing 'mold' over 'mould' quietly signals a US-domestic supplier to a Russian, Turkish or Gulf buyer. Pick British convention and never mix the two spellings on one site.
perLanguageTop.ru: Translating 'tooling' as инструменты or оборудование instead of оснастка, and 'core' as сердечник instead of пуансон. Either one identifies the page as machine-translated to any Russian moulder within a sentence.
perLanguageTop.hy: Writing purist Academy Armenian that the actual buyer cannot read. Armenia's tooling vocabulary is Russian-derived (պրես-ֆորմա, դոպուսկ, խառատային). Use native Armenian in prose with the Russian-derived term in parentheses on first mention — and end sentences with ։, not a full stop.
perLanguageTop.tr: Inverted decimal/thousands separators (1.000 vs 1,000) and the Turkish dotted-İ casing bug from text-transform without lang="tr". Both are silent, both are immediately visible to a Turkish reader. Vocabulary-wise: 'göz' for cavity, never boşluk.
perLanguageTop.th: Setting Thai in a looped government-document face (Sarabun) and with Latin line-height, which clips tone marks. Vocabulary-wise: unqualified แม่พิมพ์ (which also idiomatically means 'role model'), and the Buddhist-Era year ambiguity on 'Since 2006'.
perLanguageTop.zh: Mixing Taiwanese Traditional vocabulary (射出模具, 模座, 毛邊) into a Simplified page, and letting a Japanese font resolve for Han text. Commercially: generic quality claims are discounted instantly by a market that knows tooling costs precisely.
perLanguageTop.ur: Over-translation. Inventing pure-Urdu tooling terms (سانچہ, خلا) produces text that is correct and unreadable to Pakistani practitioners, who work in English terms. Use مولڈ, کیویٹی, رنر. And use ۔ not '.' — it is the single highest-leverage character on the page.
perLanguageTop.ar: Global letter-spacing shattering the cursive joins, and اللدائن (academic) used where the trade says البلاستيك. Also الإنتاج الضخم for mass production, which reads as propaganda.
perLanguageTop.fa: Lost ZWNJ (U+200C) turning قالب‌گیری into قالبگیری and می‌شود into میشود — the highest-frequency Persian bug, and it makes the page read as illiterate. Vocabulary-wise: مغز instead of ماهیچه for core, and گارانتی instead of ضمانت in contractual sentences.

digitPolicy.decision: Western Arabic digits (0–9) in all nine locales, without exception, including Urdu, Arabic and Persian.
rationale: This is a technical B2B site. Every number on it — wall thickness 1.8 mm, tolerance ±0.05, tonnage 500 t, cavitation 8, tool life 1 000 000 shots, steel grade 1.2344, neck standard PCO 1881, PET preform 24.5 g — sits adjacent to a Latin unit, a Latin standard designation or a Latin grade code. Eastern digits next to Latin units force the reader to switch numeral systems mid-scan.

Persian and Urdu genuinely differ between prose and technical registers: prose (newspapers, literature, general web) uses Eastern digits ۰۱۲۳۴۵۶۷۸۹, while engineering drawings, specifications, catalogues, invoices and export documents use Western digits. A page that writes ۴۸ ساعت in the hero and 0.15 mm in the spec table is internally inconsistent — and the spec table is the part that cannot change.

Arabic is split geographically: Eastern digits ٠١٢٣ dominate in Egypt and parts of the Gulf, Western digits across the Maghreb, in Levantine business writing and in essentially all international commerce. Western digits are the only choice that reads correctly across the whole Arabic-speaking market.

The codebase already encodes this: every locale in src/i18n/locales.ts is set to numerals: 'latn', with the comment that Eastern digits 'would read as consumer-facing and complicate scanning'. This reference confirms that decision rather than revisiting it.
Searchability and data entry: buyers copy part numbers, tonnages and standards out of the page into RFQs and ERP systems. Eastern digits break that copy path.
digitPolicy.safestChoice: Western digits everywhere. If a marketing-led exception is ever wanted for Persian or Urdu, confine it to a purely rhetorical number in display type (a headline count of years or projects) and never let it touch a specification, tolerance, dimension, tonnage, shot count, standard designation or date. Do not mix within a single page section.

tr.warning: Inverted vs English. Highest-consequence number bug on the site.

zh.note: Add a thin space between Han characters and adjoining Latin digits; append 年 to years (2006 年).

ar.note: Numbers stay LTR inside RTL text — isolate the run so units and parentheses do not migrate.

fa.thousands: . (period) is the Iranian convention; comma also seen — pick one

implementation: Set the numbering system explicitly rather than trusting font or locale defaults: font-variant-numeric and, where Intl is used, the -u-nu-latn extension on the locale tag (e.g. new Intl.NumberFormat('fa-u-nu-latn')). Intl.NumberFormat('fa') alone will emit Eastern digits.
Use tabular figures for every spec table and number-led stat so digits align in columns.
Non-breaking space between value and unit in all nine (500 t, 48 ساعت, 1,000 模次) so a number never orphans across a line break.
In ar/fa/ur, wrap numeric+unit runs in a bidi isolate so the unit stays attached to its number.

universal: Sell competence, not enthusiasm. In every one of these nine markets the reader is an engineer or a buyer who discounts adjectives and reads numbers. One concrete figure (tool life in shots, cycle time in seconds, tonnage, steel grade) is worth a paragraph of adjectives.

Name the constraint alongside the capability. Stating that warranty terms are per-project, or that tool life depends on resin abrasiveness, reads as expertise in all nine languages; an unqualified promise reads as a sales pitch in all nine.

Keep one term per concept across the whole site, per language. If the CTA says 'technical evaluation' the body copy must not say 'technical review' — in translation this multiplies, and a page using three words for one service stops looking like a service.
Formal address everywhere: вы, Դուք, siz, คุณ, 您, آپ, حضرتكم/plural formal, شما. Never the informal form in any of the nine.
No exclamation marks in body copy. Russian, Chinese, Arabic and Persian business writing all read them as shouting or hard selling.

Latin technical designations are a trust signal, not an untranslated string: steel grades, mould base brands, hot-runner brands, neck standards, file formats, ISO/DIN references. Use more of them, not fewer.

byLanguage.en: Declarative and unhedged, British spelling, sentence case. Terse is credible. Avoid superlatives entirely — this audience discounts them automatically.
byLanguage.ru: Formal вы, no exclamation marks, verbal-noun and passive constructions where English uses imperatives. Russian industrial buyers are actively suspicious of adjectival marketing and respond to process names and figures. Avoid качественный as a standalone claim — it is the most devalued word in Russian B2B. Use серийное (not массовое), поставка (not доставка), оснастка (not инструменты).
byLanguage.hy: Formal Դուք, more explicitly courteous than Russian. Armenia's sector is small and relationship-driven — write as an invitation to a working conversation, not as a catalogue. Native Armenian in prose, Russian-derived shop terms in parentheses on first use, Latin acronyms untouched. End sentences with ։.
byLanguage.tr: Formal siz, warm but businesslike; 'Firmamız olarak…' constructions are expected and a purely clipped Anglo style reads cold. Do NOT explain injection moulding — Türkiye has a major domestic mould sector and the reader is a peer. Native Turkish tooling vocabulary throughout (kalıp, göz, maça, yolluk, itici, çapak) rather than English imports.
byLanguage.th: Polite formal, declarative, without spoken particles (ครับ/ค่ะ) in body copy. Thai buyers in the EEC plastics cluster are used to Japanese and Taiwanese suppliers and expect precision plus visible courtesy. Transliterated English for mould components is normal and expected — pure-Thai coinages read academic.
byLanguage.zh: Dense and specification-forward; Chinese B2B copy tolerates high information density and long noun compounds. The reader may be a competitor. Avoid consumer-marketing uplift vocabulary (匠心, 赋能, empty 一站式). The persuasive content is the reason to buy OUTSIDE China: second-source risk, tariff exposure, IP terms, proximity to the customer's plant. Simplified Mainland vocabulary only.
byLanguage.ur: Formal آپ, courteous, softened imperatives (…بھیج دیجیے rather than a bare …بھیجیں). Much Pakistani B2B runs in English, so the Urdu page's job is accessibility and trust rather than being the sole technical reference — keep English terms and let the Urdu carry warmth and clarity.
byLanguage.ar: Modern Standard Arabic, never dialect. Formal but clear — the ornate honorific register of older correspondence now reads dated in procurement. Passive and impersonal constructions (تُحدَّد, يتم) are correct for terms and process descriptions. Use البلاستيك (trade) over اللدائن (academic) in commercial copy.
byLanguage.fa: Formal شما, complete sentences, more elaborate courtesy than English. The reader is likely a knowledgeable peer from a real domestic قالب‌سازی sector. Payment, shipping and documentation terms carry disproportionate weight in this market — being explicit about international delivery and paperwork persuades more here than anywhere else on the site. Use ضمانت in legal copy, گارانتی only in commercial copy.

registerGuidance.toneCalibrationForThisBusiness: The offer is 'send us anything and we will take it to production, and we can be your second source'. That proposition is trust-limited, not information-limited: the reader's real question is whether their drawing is safe and whether the supplier will still be there at T3. So confidentiality, accountability (one named partner, one contact), and specificity about what happens next do more work than capability lists in every one of the nine languages. The 'Send whatever you have' message is the emotional core and is also the phrase most damaged by literal translation — treat its rendering in each language as a design decision, not a string.
